- The first experiment successfully separated the models. Mechanisms involving second-order catalyst interactions (M19, M18, M13, M2) and substrate-induced deactivation (M11) emerged as the top candidates, showing significantly better fits (lower NLL) than standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) or product-inhibition models.
- My aim of establishing a baseline and clustering the mechanisms was achieved. We now have a clear set of leading hypotheses that share non-linear catalyst or substrate dependencies.

<hypothesis>
To distinguish between the top candidates (M19, M18, M13, M2, M11), we need to manipulate the ratio of free catalyst [cat] to substrate-bound catalyst [catS]. 
By increasing the initial catalyst concentration to its maximum (0.2) and lowering the substrate concentration (0.5), we increase the overall frequency of catalyst-catalyst encounters while ensuring a significant fraction of the catalyst remains in the free state [cat].
- Mechanisms dependent on free catalyst squared, such as M13 (2cat -> inactive) and M2 (2cat <=> cat2), will be strongly amplified due to the high [cat].
- Mechanism M18 (2catS -> inactive) depends on [catS]^2, so its deactivation rate will be suppressed compared to a high-substrate condition.
- Mechanism M19 (cat + catS -> inactive) requires both species, so its deactivation profile will be distinct, peaking when [cat] and [catS] are balanced.
- Mechanism M11 (S + cat -> inactive) will have a reduced deactivation rate due to the lower initial substrate concentration.
This design avoids extreme saturation or depletion, instead shifting the catalyst's resting state to effectively pull apart the leading hypotheses.
</hypothesis>
